periods.activity_title: Folding and Cutting Letters to Find Symmetry

tasks_in_class.description: Which of the alphabet cutouts E N X T K V O can be made by drawing half or quarter of the letter? Draw lines of symmetry on the letters.
Use lines of symmetry to make paper cutouts of diya, boat, and other designs shown on the border of the page.

time_bands.activity: Students fold a square sheet in half and then in quarters, crease the folds firmly, and discuss what the fold-line represents. The class names the fold-line a line of symmetry and recalls that the two halves match exactly when folded.

Let Us Do, p.136 ("Which of E N X T K V O can be made by drawing half or quarter…."). Students fold paper, sketch half or a quarter of each letter on the folded edge, cut, and unfold. They draw the line(s) of symmetry directly on the unfolded letter and record which letters needed one fold and which needed two.

Let Us Do, p.136 ("Use lines of symmetry to make paper cutouts of diya, boat, and other designs…."). Students choose two or three border designs, plan the fold, cut, and unfold to check whether the result matches the printed shape. Pairs compare their cutouts and identify the line of symmetry on each.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is cutting on the wrong edge — students cut the open edge instead of the fold, producing two separate halves rather than a complete letter. Prompt them to trace where the fold sits before cutting. Additional practice: Let Us Do T-2, p.136 (horizontal, vertical, and both lines of symmetry) can be assigned as independent sorting once T-1 cutouts are complete.
materials: Square paper sheets (at least four per student)

section_titles: Making a Windmill Firki — Rotational Symmetry Introduced
periods.activity_title: Sorting Letter Symmetry, Then Building a Firki

tasks_in_class.description: Which letters have a horizontal line of symmetry? Which have a vertical line of symmetry? Which have both vertical and horizontal lines of symmetry?

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Make a Windmill Firki, p.137
tasks_in_class.description: Follow the nine steps to make your own windmill firki using a square paper, scissors, and a pin on a stick or straw.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Make a Windmill Firki, p.137
tasks_in_class.description: Observe the dot in the firki. Does the firki look the same after ¼, ½, ¾, and a full turn?

time_bands.activity: Let Us Do, p.136 ("Which letters have a horizontal line of symmetry? Which have a vertical?…."). Students spread their cutouts from the folding-and-cutting work on their desks and sort them into three groups: horizontal symmetry only, vertical symmetry only, and both. The class shares findings and agrees on a sorted list.

Let Us Make a Windmill Firki, p.137 ("Follow the nine steps to make your own windmill firki…."). Students read the nine steps in the textbook, fold a square diagonally twice, cut along the four fold lines to the halfway point, and fold alternate corners to the centre. The teacher pins each firki onto a stick or straw as students complete them.

Let Us Make a Windmill Firki, p.137 ("Observe the dot in the firki. Does the firki look the same after ¼, ½, ¾, and a full turn?"). Each student marks a dot on one blade, holds the firki at arm's length, and slowly turns it, pausing at each quarter-turn to check whether the dot's position looks the same. The class records Yes/No for each fractional turn.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who have explored reflection symmetry through paper folding are now ready to meet a different question: does a shape look the same when you turn it? The firki makes this question concrete — mark a single dot and watch where it lands after each quarter-turn. A common error is spinning the firki too fast; encourage slow, deliberate quarter-turn pauses so the observation is clear.
materials: Pencils or markers for the dot

section_titles: Rotational Symmetry in Letters and Digits
periods.activity_title: Turning Letters and Reading Digit Symmetry

tasks_in_class.description: Observe letters H, I, X, Y at ¼, ½, ¾, and full turns; complete the rotational symmetry table for each letter.
Find symmetry in digits 1–9 and 0: which have reflection symmetry? Which have rotational symmetry? Which have both?

homework.description: Do the numbers 11 and 1001 have rotational symmetry, reflection symmetry, or both symmetries?

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes the term 'rotational symmetry' on the board and revisits the firki observation: the firki looked the same at every quarter-turn, which means it has rotational symmetry. The class agrees on a working definition: a shape has rotational symmetry if it looks identical at some fractional turn less than a full turn.

Let Us Do, p.138 ("Observe letters H, I, X, Y at ¼, ½, ¾, and full turns; complete the rotational symmetry table…."). Students cut out or trace each letter, mark a reference dot, and physically rotate the cut-out or use tracing paper to check at each turn. They complete the table with Yes/No entries and note which fractional turn gives a match.

Let Us Do, p.138 ("Find symmetry in digits 1–9 and 0: which have reflection symmetry? Which have rotational symmetry? Which have both?"). Students draw each digit on a small card or in their notebooks, then test each for both types of symmetry — folding for reflection, rotating for rotational — and record in a two-column table. The class pools results and resolves any disagreements by demonstration.

periods.teacher_notes: The firki observation established that 'same after a quarter-turn' is rotational symmetry; this unit asks students to apply that test to static visual objects — letters and digits. A common error is confusing a letter that looks similar with one that looks identical after turning — for example, Y looks similar at a half-turn but is actually upside-down and not the same; encourage students to mark a reference dot to detect this difference. T-8 (numbers 11 and 1001) is assigned as homework to extend the digit findings to multi-digit numbers.
materials: Small letter/digit cards or tracing paper

section_titles: Rotational Symmetry in Letters and Digits

tasks_in_class.description: Give examples of 2-, 3-, and 4-digit numbers that have rotational symmetry, reflection symmetry, or both.

time_bands.activity: The homework task on 11 and 1001 is discussed as a class. The teacher draws 11 on the board, asks a student to explain why it has rotational symmetry (both digits are '1', which has rotational symmetry, and the number reads the same when rotated 180°), and another to explain its reflection symmetry. The class uses this as a model for the day's reasoning.

Let Us Do, p.138 ("Give examples of 2-, 3-, and 4-digit numbers that have rotational symmetry, reflection symmetry, or both."). Working in pairs, students draw on their digit-symmetry table to choose digits that qualify, then combine them and test the resulting numbers. They aim for at least one example in each category for 2-digit and one for 3-digit numbers.

Pairs share their best examples. The class checks each suggestion by rotating and reflecting on the board. The teacher notes any numbers that qualify for both categories and asks: 'What is special about the digits in those numbers?' — guiding students to articulate the pattern.

periods.teacher_notes: The digit-symmetry table built in the previous work is the foundation here — students who can recall which digits have each type of symmetry can systematically construct qualifying numbers. A common error is placing a digit that lacks rotational symmetry inside a number and still claiming the whole number has rotational symmetry; prompt students to test the whole number after rotating, not just the individual digits. This is also where the fraction concept (half-turn = 180°) becomes a precise tool.
materials: Students' digit-symmetry tables from previous work

section_titles: Making Designs with Rotational and Reflection Symmetry
periods.activity_title: Checking and Modifying the Cross Design

tasks_in_class.description: Does the given cross-shaped design (circle with four directional triangles) have rotational symmetry? Yes/No.
Change the design by adding shapes so the new design looks the same after a ½ turn. Draw the new design in your notebook.
Modify or add more shapes so the new design looks the same after ¼ turn. Draw the new design in your notebook.
Do the new designs have reflection symmetry? If yes, draw the lines of symmetry.

time_bands.activity: Making Designs (a), p.139 ("Does the given cross-shaped design have rotational symmetry?"). Students look at the cross design in the textbook, mark a reference point, and decide at which fractional turns — if any — the design looks the same. They record Yes/No and name the turn.

Making Designs (b), p.139 ("Change the design by adding shapes so the new design looks the same after a ½ turn…."). Students sketch the original design in their notebooks and experiment with adding shapes. They check each trial by mentally (or physically, with tracing paper) rotating it half a turn before finalising their drawing.

Making Designs (c), p.139 ("Modify or add more shapes so the new design looks the same after ¼ turn…."). Students take their half-turn design and further modify it, this time targeting quarter-turn symmetry. They sketch the result and compare with a partner to verify the symmetry holds at all four quarter-turns.

Making Designs (d), p.139 ("Do the new designs have reflection symmetry? If yes, draw the lines of symmetry."). Students look at their modified designs and test for reflection symmetry by folding or drawing fold-lines. They draw any lines of symmetry they find and share one finding with the class.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who have classified symmetry in letters and digits are now moving from observer to designer — the shift from recognising a property to deliberately building it into a new design. A common error is adding a shape to one side without its corresponding copy, so the half-turn test fails; remind students that for half-turn symmetry, every part of the design must have a matching part at the opposite side of the centre. The link to fractions is explicit: half-turn and quarter-turn are the measuring language.

section_titles: Making Designs with Rotational and Reflection Symmetry
periods.activity_title: Colouring for Quarter-Turn Symmetry and Free Design Making

tasks_in_class.description: Does the 2-colour 2×2 square design look the same after ½ turn? Does it look the same after ¼ turn?
Colour the given star-grid square using two colours so the design looks the same after every ¼ turn. How many times does the shape look the same during a full turn?
Cut out squares and equilateral triangles (same side length, from end of book) and make different symmetrical designs using these two shapes.
Do the designs made from squares and triangles have reflection symmetry also? Draw the line(s) of symmetry.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Think, p.139 ("Does the 2-colour 2×2 square design look the same after ½ turn? Does it look the same after ¼ turn?"). Students look at the printed 2×2 design, mark a corner dot, and test each fractional turn. They record findings and discuss why the half-turn works but the quarter-turn might not.

Let Us Think, p.139 ("Colour the given star-grid square using two colours so the design looks the same after every ¼ turn…."). Students plan their colouring before they commit — they identify which cells map onto which others after a quarter-turn, then colour accordingly. They count how many times the design looks the same in a full turn and write the answer.

Let Us Do, p.139 ("Cut out squares and equilateral triangles…and make different symmetrical designs…."). Students cut out the shapes from the back of the textbook and arrange them on a plain sheet, experimenting with different configurations. They aim to make at least two distinct designs, each with some form of symmetry.

Let Us Do, p.139 ("Do the designs made from squares and triangles have reflection symmetry also? Draw the line(s) of symmetry."). Students look at their two designs and draw in any lines of reflection symmetry. The class briefly shares: 'Does anyone have a design with both types of symmetry?'

periods.teacher_notes: The 2×2 colouring task is a bridge between reasoning about given designs and creating new ones; students who see why quarter-turn symmetry demands four matching cells are better prepared to design freely with cut shapes. A common error in the star-grid task is colouring opposite cells the same colour without checking the quarter-turn, which gives half-turn symmetry only; prompt students to rotate the grid 90° and compare cell positions before colouring. The cut-shape activity is intentionally open — varied outcomes are expected and desirable.
materials: Pencils and at least two colours per student
Plain paper for arranging cut shapes
Glue sticks (optional, to fix final designs)

section_titles: Block Printing — Symmetry in Cultural Context
periods.activity_title: Exploring Block Printing and Classifying Symmetry

tasks_in_class.description: Does the composite shape (two triangles flanking a 2×2 square) have reflection symmetry? Draw lines. Does it have rotational symmetry? At which turn? Does it have both?
Match each wooden block (i–v) to its correct print (a–e) by drawing a line. One is done for you.
Observe shapes on the border of the page. Put a ✓ on shapes with reflection symmetry. Put a * on shapes with rotational symmetry.

time_bands.activity: The teacher briefly describes Rajasthan block printing: an artisan carves a wooden block and stamps it repeatedly to form a fabric pattern. The class looks at the block-printing images on p.140 and discusses what symmetry properties a repeated stamp might create.

Let Us Explore, p.140 ("Does the composite shape — two triangles flanking a 2×2 square — have reflection symmetry? Draw lines. Does it have rotational symmetry? At which turn?"). Students draw the shape in their notebooks, test it for reflection by drawing fold-lines, then test for rotational symmetry by marking a reference point and rotating. They record all symmetry properties found.

Let Us Explore, p.140 ("Match each wooden block (i–v) to its correct print (a–e) by drawing a line…."). Students study how a carved block, when pressed on paper, produces a mirror image. They work through each block, reasoning about which print it must generate, and draw the matching lines systematically.

Let Us Do, p.141 ("Observe shapes on the border of the page. Put a ✓ on shapes with reflection symmetry. Put a * on shapes with rotational symmetry."). Students work through each border shape, applying both tests and marking the appropriate symbol. Pairs compare and resolve any differences.

periods.teacher_notes: The block-to-print matching task is the key conceptual moment: a block is not symmetric itself, but the act of stamping creates a mirror image — this connects the craft to the mathematical idea of reflection symmetry in a tangible way. A common error is marking a printed shape as identical to the block rather than its mirror; prompt students to trace the block shape and flip the tracing to see the print. T-19 (sorting designs into three symmetry categories) is closely related and can be noted as additional discussion: Let Us Explore, p.140.

section_titles: Block Printing — Symmetry in Cultural Context
periods.activity_title: Completing Block Symmetry Tasks and Vegetable Printing

tasks_in_class.description: Sort your designs into three categories: designs with only rotational symmetry, only reflection symmetry, and both rotational and reflection symmetry.
Design B: fill in 'The design B looks the same after every __ turn. This design has __ symmetry.'
Create symmetrical patterns and designs using vegetable blocks (okra, potato). Some examples are shown.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Explore, p.140 ("Sort your designs into three categories: only rotational symmetry, only reflection symmetry, and both…."). Students use their notes and observations from the composite-shape and border-shape tasks to sort. The class builds a shared three-column tally on the board.

Let Us Do, p.141 ("Design B: fill in 'The design B looks the same after every __ turn. This design has __ symmetry.'"). Students examine Design B on p.141, mark a reference point, and determine the smallest fractional turn at which it looks the same. They complete the sentence and share their answer with a partner.

Project Work, p.141 ("Create symmetrical patterns and designs using vegetable blocks — okra, potato…."). Students cut okra or potato halves (pre-cut by the teacher before the unit), apply paint or ink, and stamp repeated prints on plain paper. They experiment with orientations to create patterns that have reflection symmetry, rotational symmetry, or both, then annotate their prints with the symmetry type.

periods.teacher_notes: Sorting designs into three symmetry categories consolidates the two symmetry types as distinct, comparable properties — students must hold both definitions in mind simultaneously. A common error in the vegetable printing activity is stamping randomly and then attempting to claim symmetry afterwards; encourage students to plan the stamp orientation before printing, drawing a light pencil guide if needed. This unit completes all chapter sections so the synthesis unit can draw on the full range of concepts.

periods.activity_title: Chapter Synthesis — Two Symmetries, One Chapter

time_bands.activity: The class draws a two-column chart on paper: 'Reflection Symmetry' and 'Rotational Symmetry'. Working from memory, students list at least three objects or ideas from the chapter that show each type. Pairs compare lists and add any entries the other missed. The teacher collects responses on the board to form a shared class chart.

The teacher poses a design challenge: 'Invent a single design — made with lines and simple shapes — that has both a vertical line of symmetry and half-turn rotational symmetry.' Students sketch independently, then share with a neighbour who tests both properties using the fold-and-rotate method. The class discusses which entries satisfy both conditions and why.

The teacher displays (or writes on the board) a short set of four multi-digit numbers and asks: for each, does it have reflection symmetry, rotational symmetry, both, or neither? Students reason from their knowledge of digit symmetry and the combining rule. Each student writes a brief justification — not just the answer — and one student per number explains to the class.

The class revisits the block-printing idea: the teacher stamps (or sketches) a simple asymmetric shape four times around a centre point and asks, 'What symmetry does the combined print have that the single stamp does not?' Students identify the rotational symmetry of the whole pattern and any lines of reflection symmetry that appeared. The unit closes with students naming one thing from the chapter they found surprising.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis draws together reflection symmetry from alphabet cutouts and paper folding, rotational symmetry from the firki and letter-turn table, digit-number combining from the symmetry investigation, design creation from the grid and cut-shape work, and the block-printing context — naming each by its content rather than by any earlier activity. A common error at synthesis stage is conflating 'looks similar' with 'looks the same' after turning; the reference-dot technique from the firki work is the most reliable corrective. Encourage students to use precise fractional-turn language throughout.
materials: Board and chalk/marker for the teacher

items.prompt: Fold a square piece of paper in half along a vertical line. Draw and cut out half of the letter T on the folded edge, then unfold. Describe the shape you get and draw the line of symmetry on it.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Unfolding gives a complete letter T with a vertical line of symmetry running down its centre. The line of symmetry divides the T into two mirror-image halves.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fold the paper so the fold-line is the line of symmetry; cut half the letter on the fold; unfold to reveal the whole letter.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student use real paper, fold, and cut before drawing. Stretch: ask them to find a second letter that needs two folds and explain why.

exercise.description: Use lines of symmetry to make paper cutouts of diya, boat, and other designs shown on the border of the page.

items.section_title: Making a Windmill Firki — Rotational Symmetry Introduced
items.prompt: A windmill firki is made from a square paper by folding and cutting. A dot is marked on one blade. After which fractional turns does the firki look exactly the same as it did at the start?

options.label: A
options.text: After ¼ turn, ½ turn, ¾ turn, and a full turn

options.label: B
options.text: It never looks the same until a full turn

options.label: C
options.text: Only after a full turn

options.label: D
options.text: Only after a ½ turn and a full turn

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The firki looks the same after every quarter-turn — at ¼, ½, ¾, and a full turn.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Mark a reference dot, rotate by one quarter-turn at a time, and check whether the firki's appearance is identical at each stop.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student thinks rotational symmetry requires a full turn only, missing the idea that fractional turns can also return a shape to an identical appearance.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student recognises half-turn symmetry but has not noticed that the four-bladed firki also looks the same at quarter and three-quarter turns.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student confuses rotational symmetry with a full rotation, not understanding that the shape can look identical at turns smaller than 360°.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student hold a real firki and pause at each quarter-turn to look. Stretch: ask how many times the firki looks the same in one full turn and write that number.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Make a Windmill Firki, p.137
exercise.description: Follow the nine steps to make your own windmill firki using a square paper, scissors, and a pin on a stick or straw.

items.section_title: Making Designs with Rotational and Reflection Symmetry
items.prompt: A star-grid square is divided into 8 equal parts. You want to colour it with two colours so that the design looks exactly the same after every ¼ turn. How many parts must share the same colour? Explain your reasoning.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Each ¼ turn moves every part to a new position, so the four positions one part visits in a full turn must all be the same colour. With 8 parts and 2 colours, 4 parts get colour 1 and 4 parts get colour 2, arranged so that rotating by ¼ always maps colour 1 onto colour 1 and colour 2 onto colour 2.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify which parts map onto each other under a ¼ turn and assign the same colour to each group of four.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a simple 4-cell square and ask which cells swap at a ¼ turn before tackling the 8-part grid. Stretch: ask whether the same colouring also gives reflection symmetry, and if so, how many lines.

exercise.description: Colour the given star-grid square using two colours so the design looks the same after every ¼ turn. How many times does the shape look the same during a full turn?

items.section_title: Making Designs with Rotational and Reflection Symmetry
items.prompt: Using only squares and equilateral triangles of the same side length, arrange the shapes to make a design that has at least one line of reflection symmetry. Sketch your design and draw the line of symmetry on it.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any arrangement where the shapes on the left of a central fold-line are the mirror image of the shapes on the right (or top mirrors bottom) is correct. A common valid example: one square in the centre with one triangle on each of its left and right sides, giving a vertical line of symmetry.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place shapes on one side of a fold-line, then mirror them exactly on the other side; the fold-line is the line of symmetry.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student cut and physically arrange real shapes, fold the paper to check before drawing. Stretch: modify the design so it also has half-turn rotational symmetry and show both symmetries.

exercise.description: Cut out squares and equilateral triangles (same side length, from end of book) and make different symmetrical designs using these two shapes.

items.section_title: Block Printing — Symmetry in Cultural Context
items.prompt: An artisan stamps an okra slice in paint and presses it four times around a central point, turning the paper by a ¼ turn between each stamp. Will the finished print have rotational symmetry? Name the fractional turn at which it will look the same.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes, the finished print will have rotational symmetry. It will look the same after every ¼ turn — at ¼, ½, ¾, and a full turn — because each stamp is placed at exactly one quarter-turn from the previous one.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Since the pattern repeats every ¼ turn and four stamps complete a full turn, the print looks the same at every ¼-turn stop.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to draw four identical small shapes around a dot, each rotated ¼ turn from the last, and look at the result. Stretch: ask whether the print also has reflection symmetry, and what property of the okra shape would determine this.

exercise.description: Create symmetrical patterns and designs using vegetable blocks (okra, potato). Some examples are shown.

items.prompt: Which of these letters can be cut from a single sheet of paper folded once along a vertical line and once along a horizontal line (folded into quarters)?

options.label: A
options.text: E

options.label: B
options.text: H

options.label: C
options.text: N

options.label: D
options.text: V

teacher_guide.expected_answer: H. The letter H has both a vertical and a horizontal line of symmetry, so folding into quarters and cutting yields the full letter when unfolded.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A letter that needs two folds must have both a vertical and a horizontal line of symmetry; test each letter for both symmetries.

what_each_option_reveals.C: N has no line of symmetry, so it cannot be made by any fold-and-cut method; the student may be guessing rather than testing.
what_each_option_reveals.A: E has a horizontal line of symmetry but not a vertical one, so only one fold works; the student has not checked both symmetries.
what_each_option_reveals.D: V has a vertical line of symmetry but not a horizontal one; the student has not checked for the second symmetry needed for a quarter-fold.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student trace each letter, draw any fold-lines they can find, and count them before deciding. Stretch: name one more letter from the alphabet that also needs two folds.

exercise.description: Which of the alphabet cutouts E N X T K V O can be made by drawing half or quarter of the letter? Draw lines of symmetry on the letters.

items.prompt:
Sort the letters below into three groups: only vertical line of symmetry, only horizontal line of symmetry, and both. Write each letter in the correct group.

Letters: A, B, H, V, C, X

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Only vertical: A, V. Only horizontal: B, C. Both: H, X.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Draw a vertical fold-line and check if the two halves match; then draw a horizontal fold-line and check again; assign each letter based on which test(s) pass.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student trace each letter and physically fold the tracing to test. Stretch: find one more letter for each group from the full alphabet.

exercise.description: Which letters have a horizontal line of symmetry? Which have a vertical line of symmetry? Which have both vertical and horizontal lines of symmetry?

items.section_title: Making a Windmill Firki — Rotational Symmetry Introduced
items.prompt: A firki has 4 identical blades. After which turn does the firki first look exactly the same as when it started?

options.label: A
options.text: After a full turn only

options.label: B
options.text: After ¼ turn

options.label: C
options.text: After ½ turn

options.label: D
options.text: After ¾ turn

teacher_guide.expected_answer: After ¼ turn. Because the firki has 4 identical blades equally spaced, rotating by one quarter of a full turn brings the next blade into the original blade's position, making the firki look identical.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the full turn equally among the four blades: 1 ÷ 4 = ¼ turn is the smallest fractional turn at which the firki looks the same.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student recognises half-turn symmetry but has missed the smaller ¼-turn match that four equally-spaced blades produce.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may be guessing or confusing three-quarter with the fraction that divides four; ¾ turn does give a match but it is not the first.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student does not understand rotational symmetry and believes only a complete rotation restores the original appearance.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw four equally spaced dots on a circle and ask after how many dots the pattern repeats. Stretch: ask what the smallest matching turn would be for a firki with 6 blades.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Make a Windmill Firki, p.137
exercise.description: Observe the dot in the firki. Does the firki look the same after ¼, ½, ¾, and a full turn?

items.section_title: Rotational Symmetry in Letters and Digits
items.prompt:
Complete the table for the letters H and Y.

For each letter, write YES or NO: Does it have rotational symmetry at ¼ turn? At ½ turn?
items.visual_stimulus:
| Letter | Same after ¼ turn? | Same after ½ turn? |
| H | ... | ... |
| Y | ... | ... |

teacher_guide.expected_answer: H: No at ¼ turn, Yes at ½ turn. Y: No at ¼ turn, No at ½ turn (Y rotated 180° is an upside-down Y, not the same letter).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Mark a reference dot on the letter, rotate by the stated fraction, and check whether every part of the letter lands in the same position as before.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: trace the letters onto tracing paper, mark a dot, and physically rotate before filling the table. Stretch: add a row for X and I and complete those entries too.

exercise.description: Observe letters H, I, X, Y at ¼, ½, ¾, and full turns; complete the rotational symmetry table for each letter.

items.section_title: Rotational Symmetry in Letters and Digits
items.prompt: The digit 8 has both reflection symmetry and rotational symmetry at a ½ turn. Using only digits that share at least one of these symmetry properties, write one 3-digit number that has rotational symmetry at ½ turn. Explain why your number qualifies.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A valid answer is 808 (or 818, 888, 180, 108, etc., provided all digits have ½-turn rotational symmetry and the whole number looks the same when rotated 180°). For example, 808 rotated 180° reads 808 — digit 0 rotated is 0, digit 8 rotated is 8, and the order reverses to give the same string.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Each digit must look the same at a ½ turn, and when the whole number is rotated 180° the digit order reverses — check that the reversed sequence still reads the same number.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student the list of digits that have ½-turn rotational symmetry (0, 1, 8) and ask them to arrange two or three of them. Stretch: find a 4-digit number with both rotational and reflection symmetry.

exercise.description: Give examples of 2-, 3-, and 4-digit numbers that have rotational symmetry, reflection symmetry, or both.

items.section_title: Making Designs with Rotational and Reflection Symmetry
items.prompt: A 2×2 square is coloured with two colours: the top-left and bottom-right cells are red; the top-right and bottom-left cells are blue. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It does not look the same after any fractional turn

options.label: B
options.text: It looks the same after both ¼ turn and ½ turn

options.label: C
options.text: It looks the same after ¼ turn but not after ½ turn

options.label: D
options.text: It looks the same after ½ turn but not after ¼ turn

teacher_guide.expected_answer: It looks the same after a ½ turn but not after a ¼ turn. A ½ turn swaps each cell with its diagonally opposite cell — red goes to red and blue goes to blue. A ¼ turn moves each cell to a position that currently holds the other colour, so the design looks different.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Trace the colours through each fractional turn: ¼ turn maps top-left (red) to top-right (blue), so the design changes; ½ turn maps top-left (red) to bottom-right (red), so it is preserved.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has the two turns reversed, possibly confusing which rotation is smaller.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has not checked the ¼-turn carefully; they may assume any symmetric-looking design has both types.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student does not recognise that diagonally opposite colouring creates half-turn rotational symmetry.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw the 2×2 grid on paper, colour it, and physically rotate the paper by a quarter-turn to see the colour positions change. Stretch: modify the colouring so the design also has a line of reflection symmetry.

exercise.description: Does the 2-colour 2×2 square design look the same after ½ turn? Does it look the same after ¼ turn?

items.section_title: Block Printing — Symmetry in Cultural Context
items.prompt: A composite shape is made by placing one triangle on the left side of a square and one identical triangle on the right side, both pointing outward. Does this shape have a vertical line of symmetry? Does it have a horizontal line of symmetry? Give a reason for each answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes, it has a vertical line of symmetry: the vertical fold-line runs through the centre of the square and swaps the two triangles, which are identical, so both halves match. Whether it has a horizontal line depends on the triangle shape; for equilateral or symmetric triangles pointing left and right, there is also a horizontal line of symmetry if the triangles are symmetric about the horizontal axis.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Draw the fold-line and check whether the shape on each side is the mirror image of the other; repeat for the horizontal fold.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw the shape, cut it out, and fold it along both possible axes to test. Stretch: add a triangle on the top and bottom and determine whether the new shape has both lines and rotational symmetry.

exercise.description: Does the composite shape (two triangles flanking a 2×2 square) have reflection symmetry? Draw lines. Does it have rotational symmetry? At which turn? Does it have both?

items.section_title: Block Printing — Symmetry in Cultural Context
items.prompt: A wooden block has an asymmetric carved design — it has no line of symmetry and no rotational symmetry. When the artisan presses this block on fabric, what can be said about the print?

options.label: A
options.text: The print has a line of symmetry even though the block does not

options.label: B
options.text: The print has rotational symmetry even though the block does not

options.label: C
options.text: The print is a mirror image of the block design

options.label: D
options.text: The print is identical to the block design

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The print is a mirror image of the block design. Pressing a carved block onto a surface reverses left and right, producing the reflection of the original design.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Pressing an object onto a surface flips it left-to-right; the result is the mirror image, which is the same as reflection symmetry applied once.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has not considered the reversal that happens when a raised surface is pressed down; they treat stamping as copying.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student confuses the printing process with a symmetry-creating operation; a single stamp of an asymmetric block produces an asymmetric print.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student is guessing that printing adds a new symmetry property; it does not — it only reverses the design.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to write a letter on their palm with a marker and press it on paper — the letter reverses. Stretch: ask what would happen to the print if the block itself had a vertical line of symmetry.

exercise.description: Match each wooden block (i–v) to its correct print (a–e) by drawing a line. One is done for you.

items.section_title: Block Printing — Symmetry in Cultural Context
items.prompt: Design B on p.141 of your textbook looks the same after every ¼ turn. Complete the sentence: 'Design B looks the same after every ___ turn. This design has ___ symmetry.'

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Design B looks the same after every ¼ turn. This design has rotational symmetry.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the smallest fractional turn at which the design looks identical to its starting position; that fraction names the rotational symmetry.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student a printed copy of the design to physically rotate and pause at each quarter-turn. Stretch: ask how many lines of reflection symmetry the design has, if any.

exercise.description: Design B: fill in 'The design B looks the same after every __ turn. This design has __ symmetry.'
